regions.name: Southern Oregon
regions.summary: Southern Oregon is the warm, dry half of the state's wine country, an umbrella AVA approved in 2004 that joins the Umpqua Valley and the Rogue Valley. Where the Willamette Valley is built on Pinot Noir, the south grows a little of almost everything: Pinot Noir and Riesling in the cool corner at Elkton, Tempranillo, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon in the warmer valleys, and Albariño and Viognier among the whites. The mountains around it shelter the vineyards from Pacific rain, and its old, folded geology gives a patchwork of soils. A server should know it as the home of Oregon Tempranillo and of variety.

terroir.climate: Warmer and drier than the Willamette Valley, with hot summer days, cool nights and most of the rain in winter. The Coast Range and the Klamath Mountains stand between the vineyards and the Pacific, so the Rogue Valley sits in a rain shadow and often needs irrigation, while the Umpqua Valley is milder and wetter, with a cool marine reach at Elkton near the coast.
terroir.soils: The Klamath Mountains hold some of the oldest rocks in the state, a jumble of ancient seabed, volcanic and metamorphic rock lifted and folded together. The vineyards sit on alluvial benches and hillsides of clay loam, decomposed granite, schist and river gravel, which change from one valley, and often from one slope, to the next.
terroir.topography: A set of river valleys between three ranges: the Coast Range to the west, the Cascades to the east and the Klamath Mountains, the Siskiyous among them, to the south. Vineyards climb from the valley floors onto benches and foothills, generally higher in the Rogue Valley than in the Umpqua.
terroir.water: The Umpqua and the Rogue rivers drain west to the Pacific through the mountains; their valleys carry marine air inland, most strongly along the Umpqua at Elkton, and the Applegate River joins the Rogue from the south.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: The signature red of the south since the 1990s, ripe and spicy in the warm Umpqua and Rogue valleys, often aged in American and French oak.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown mostly in the cooler Umpqua Valley and at Elkton, lighter and more savoury than the Willamette's.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Dark fruited and peppery from the warm Rogue and Applegate valleys, sometimes co-fermented with a little Viognier.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted in the warmest parts of the Rogue Valley, alone or in blends with Merlot.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: A fresh, saline white that has spread through the Umpqua and Rogue valleys since the early 2000s.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: A floral white from the warm Rogue and Applegate valleys, sometimes blended into Syrah.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: An early planting of the Umpqua Valley, still grown in the cooler Elkton sites.

wines.note: Medium to full bodied, with red plum, dried cherry and leather, firm tannin and a touch of vanilla from oak; a match for grilled lamb.
Dark fruit, black pepper and smoked meat, ripe but fresh thanks to cool nights; serve it with braised short rib.
Crisp and saline with lime, peach and a light floral lift; poured with oysters and shellfish.
Light, bright red fruit and earthy, savoury notes, grown in the coolest corner of the south near the coast.

made.viticulture: Vineyards are spread thinly over a large, mountainous area, often on benches and hillsides above the valley floors. The warm, dry summers keep disease pressure lower than in the north, but frost can strike the valley floors in spring and the Rogue Valley often needs irrigation through its dry summers. Growers match the grape to the site with unusual freedom: Pinot Noir and Riesling where the marine air reaches, Tempranillo, Syrah and the Bordeaux grapes in the warm, sheltered valleys. Most vineyards are trained on vertical trellises, and many are farmed by small family estates that sell part of their crop to wineries across the state.
made.winemaking: There is no single style. Reds are fermented in open or closed tanks and aged in French and American oak, with Tempranillo often given extended time in barrel in the manner of Rioja. Syrah may be co-fermented with a little Viognier, as in the northern Rhône. Whites such as Albariño and Viognier are fermented cool in stainless steel to keep their freshness, and a few producers make traditional method sparkling wine and late harvest whites. Much of the fruit grown here is trucked north and blended into wines labelled with the broader Oregon name.

law.classification: Southern Oregon is an American Viticultural Area, a federal designation of place that says where the grapes grew and nothing about grape, yield or ageing. It contains two older AVAs, the Umpqua Valley and the Rogue Valley, and they in turn hold smaller nested AVAs. Oregon's own rules are stricter than the federal ones: a wine naming an AVA must take at least 95 per cent of its grapes from it, and most varietal wines must hold at least 90 per cent of the named grape, with a shorter list of varieties allowed at the federal 75 per cent.
tiers: The umbrella AVA approved in 2004, covering the Umpqua and Rogue valleys.
The northern valley, approved in 1984, with Elkton Oregon and Red Hill Douglas County nested inside.
The southern valley, approved in 1991, with the Applegate Valley nested inside.
labels: At least 95 per cent of the grapes from the named AVA under Oregon's rules.
At least 90 per cent of the named grape for most varieties under Oregon's rules.

places.name: Umpqua Valley
places.note: The northern valley around Roseburg, a maze of small hills and river bends where Oregon's first Pinot Noir after Prohibition was planted in 1961; today it is known for Tempranillo, Pinot Noir and Albariño.

places.name: Elkton Oregon
places.note: The coolest corner of the Umpqua, near the coast, where marine air suits Pinot Noir, Riesling and Pinot Gris.

places.name: Red Hill Douglas County
places.note: A single hill of red volcanic soil within the Umpqua Valley, one of the smallest AVAs in the country.

places.name: Rogue Valley
places.note: The southern valley along the Rogue River and its tributaries, the warmest and driest part of western Oregon, growing Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo and Viognier on benches well above the valley floor.

places.name: Applegate Valley
places.note: A side valley of the Rogue, warm by day and cooled at night by air off the Siskiyous, known for Syrah, Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon.

places.name: Roseburg
places.note: The main town of the Umpqua Valley and the centre of its wine trail, ringed by vineyards on small hills along the river and its forks, where most of the valley's wineries welcome visitors.

places.name: Medford and Ashland
places.note: The towns of the Rogue Valley, whose vineyards spread along Bear Creek and the Rogue between and around them.

producers.name: Abacela
producers.why: Planted the first commercial Tempranillo of the Pacific Northwest, in the Umpqua Valley in 1995.

producers.name: HillCrest Vineyard
producers.why: The Umpqua estate whose 1961 planting brought Pinot Noir back to Oregon after Prohibition.

producers.name: Troon Vineyard
producers.why: An Applegate Valley estate known for biodynamic farming and Rhône and Mediterranean grapes.

exam: Know that Southern Oregon joins the Umpqua and Rogue valleys under one AVA.
Tie Tempranillo to the Umpqua Valley and Abacela.
Name the nested AVAs: Elkton Oregon, Red Hill Douglas County and the Applegate Valley.
Contrast the warm, dry south with the cool, wet Willamette Valley.
traps: The Applegate Valley lies within the Rogue Valley, not the Umpqua.
Elkton Oregon is cool, unlike the rest of the south.
Southern Oregon is an AVA of its own, not just a direction on the map.

cards.f: Southern Oregon AVA: what does it cover?
cards.b: The Umpqua Valley and the Rogue Valley, under one umbrella AVA approved in 2004.

cards.f: Southern Oregon: climate compared with the Willamette
cards.b: Warmer and drier, sheltered from Pacific rain by the Coast Range and the Klamath Mountains.
Tempranillo, first planted commercially in the Pacific Northwest at Abacela in 1995.

cards.f: Rogue Valley: the grapes it grows
cards.b: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo and Viognier, in the warmest, driest part of western Oregon.

cards.f: Southern Oregon: the white rising fastest
cards.b: Albariño, crisp and saline, grown in both valleys.

cards.f: Oregon AVA labelling: minimum share from the AVA
cards.b: 95 per cent under Oregon's rules, stricter than the federal 85 per cent.

cards.f: Elkton Oregon AVA: why it is different
cards.b: It is the cool, marine corner of the Umpqua Valley, suited to Pinot Noir and Riesling.

cards.f: Red Hill Douglas County AVA: what it is
cards.b: A single hill of red volcanic soil nested within the Umpqua Valley.

questions.q: Which two valleys does the Southern Oregon AVA join?
questions.exp: Southern Oregon, approved in 2004, is the umbrella for the Umpqua Valley and the Rogue Valley; the Willamette lies to the north.

questions.q: Which red grape did Abacela pioneer in the Umpqua Valley?
questions.exp: Abacela planted the first commercial Tempranillo of the Pacific Northwest in 1995, matching the grape to a warm, dry site.

questions.q: Which nested AVA lies within the Rogue Valley?
questions.exp: The Applegate Valley is a side valley of the Rogue; Elkton Oregon and Red Hill Douglas County sit in the Umpqua, the Eola-Amity Hills in the Willamette.

questions.q: What share of its grapes must an Oregon wine take from the AVA it names?
questions.exp: Oregon asks 95 per cent from the named AVA, stricter than the federal rule of 85 per cent.

questions.q: Which mountains, with the Coast Range, shelter the Rogue Valley from Pacific rain?
questions.exp: The Klamath Mountains and the Coast Range stand between the Rogue Valley and the ocean; the Cascades rise to its east.

questions.q: In which year was the Southern Oregon AVA approved?
questions.exp: Southern Oregon became an AVA in 2004, joining the older Umpqua Valley and Rogue Valley AVAs under one name.

questions.q: Which nested AVA is the cool, marine corner of the Umpqua Valley?
questions.exp: Elkton Oregon lies near the coast, where marine air cools the vines enough for Pinot Noir and Riesling.

questions.q: Which nested AVA of the Umpqua Valley is a single hill of red volcanic soil?
questions.exp: Red Hill Douglas County is one hill within the Umpqua Valley, one of the smallest AVAs in the United States.

deeper.head: The Klamath geology
deeper.text: The Klamath Mountains are an old terrane: slices of ocean crust, volcanic island arcs and seabed sediment that were scraped onto the edge of North America and later lifted and folded. Weathering of this mixture gives the south its unusual range of soils, from serpentine and schist to granite and clay, and it explains why two neighbouring vineyards can make very different wines from the same grape.

deeper.head: The nested AVAs and their dates
deeper.text: The Umpqua Valley AVA was approved in 1984 and the Rogue Valley in 1991; the Southern Oregon AVA joined them under one name in 2004. Nested within are the Applegate Valley in the Rogue, and Red Hill Douglas County and Elkton Oregon in the Umpqua, the last of them approved in 2013. A wine may name the smallest AVA that fits its grapes.

deeper.head: Spanish grapes in Oregon
deeper.text: Tempranillo was planted in the Umpqua Valley in 1995 after a search for a site whose climate matched that of Ribera del Duero and Rioja. Its success drew Albariño, Grenache and other Iberian and Mediterranean grapes into both valleys, and it explains why the warm, dry summers and cool nights of the south suit grapes the cool, wet north cannot ripen.

Within the Rogue Valley, growers distinguish three side valleys: the Applegate to the west, the Illinois Valley, the coolest and wettest, closest to the coast, and Bear Creek, the warmest, around Medford and Ashland. Each is a different climate within the one AVA, and the wines change with them, from Pinot Noir in the Illinois Valley to Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon along Bear Creek.
